subject: soulScythe
pitch:
Category: Fantasy weapon.
Subject: dragonbone soul scythe.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a League of Legends-style dragonbone soul scythe—a tall, ornate weapon around 2.1 meters, standing upright with its base touching the floor at y=0, emphasizing glowing ethereal energy and painterly stylization.

I'm sketching the structure: a root joint anchoring the grip, a bone-white vertebrae-like shaft with a slight S-curve, a darker inner core sweep, and beaded vertebrae segments built using path-following placement to give it that organic skeletal look.

I'll simplify by setting up two joints, shaft and blade, splitting bone assignment by height so parts above a threshold belong to the blade and the rest to the shaft, passing bone explicitly in each helper call. For the blade itself I'm extruding a curved outline in the side (z,y) plane from the top of the shaft to form the scythe's wing-like shape.

The design merges two ideas: a thick, knobby bone spine along the top edge of the blade with a glowing teal soul-energy membrane hanging beneath it, going for a Thresh/Kalista/Viego-inspired Soul Reaper aesthetic with ivory bone, gold trim, and dark purple accents against the cyan glow.

I'm plotting the curve coordinates for the blade -- the spine arcs upward and forward before sweeping down to the tip, while the cutting edge traces a separate lower curve from the heel near the shaft out to that same point.

Still plotting blade coordinates...

I'm checking that the blade's width tapers correctly toward the tip without the top and bottom edges crossing, verifying the curve stays convex and consistent down to the pointed end.

Smoothing could cut corners across such thin geometry near the sharp tip, so I'll avoid smoothing entirely and instead densely sample the curves into point lists for the blade outline, keeping the tip marked explicitly sharp. Now I'm planning the spine bone sweep.

Writing spine sweep code...

Working out the rotation math...

Actually a thin extruded slab with a small depth works well — both front and back caps get the rewritten UV mapping so the texture shows on each side, with the back appearing mirrored but that's acceptable since I'll avoid putting text on it. The glow effect should still work fine on textured parts, and alpha testing lets transparent texture pixels get cut away for a wispy, translucent blade edge.

I'll place the shape using THREE.Shape from the path points, letting ExtrudeGeometry handle winding direction automatically, and scale up for the glow effect. For the blade's layered look, I'm thinking of a dragon-wing bone structure—three tapered struts radiating from the heel to points along the spine, like finger bones supporting a membrane, giving it that soul-energy wing aesthetic.

Now I'm defining the strut placement across the glow plane with slightly thicker radius so they read on both sides, plus a bright white-teal cutting edge ribbon along the bottom curve and a thick knobbed spine bone that tapers into a clawed tip. Setting up the coordinate mapping function for the blade curves in model space to start plotting the top curve points.

Still plotting curve points...

For the outline, I'm sampling the top curve from heel to tip, then the bottom curve reversed from tip back to heel, closing the loop at the starting heel point.

Writing coordinate derivation and strut sweep logic...

I also want a glowing bright white-teal honed edge along the bottom cutting sweep. Now for the signature piece — a dragon skull at the shaft heel below the blade, jaws gripping the shaft, horns swept back, glowing teal soul-fire eyes, facing forward and slightly down, roughly 0.22m long with separate upper and lower jaw pieces.

I'm positioning the skull center around [0,1.7,0.08], checking it clears the blade's inner edge, and letting the horns sweep back behind the shaft so they don't clash with the skull's silhouette. Now I'm blocking out the cranium shape as a scaled sphere-like form at that center point.

Still writing skull geometry...

Setting up skull and jaw joints with proper parenting, then planning teeth as rows of downward-pointing spikes on the upper snout and upward-pointing spikes on the lower jaw, mirrored on both sides.

Now I'm working out the shaft geometry, running from the grip area down to the butt end, with the base terminating in a clawed cap gripping a small glowing orb for a decorative flourish.

Still shaping the talons...

For the rig, I'm structuring a joint hierarchy: a root "scythe" joint, then "blade" and "skull" children, with bottom parts auto-assigned to the nearest joint by height. I'm now sketching the shaft as a smooth catmull-rom curve running up through several control points along the y-axis.

Making the shaft look like stacked vertebrae using a lathed bead profile, repeated along the curve with shared geometry for efficiency...

I'm spacing out roughly 17 vertebrae with small gaps between them so a thin glowing teal core at the center shows through, like a soul-glow running through dragon bone.

Now I'm adding tiny spines jutting backward from alternating vertebrae, and designing a wrapped grip section mid-shaft with a dark cloth texture, stripes, and gold rings, placing vertebrae only outside that grip zone along the shaft's path.

For positioning, I'm finding each vertebra's point and tangent along the shaft using closestT and aligning the bone geometry's default y-axis to that tangent, which sidesteps earlier orientation issues. I'm also tapering vertebra size slightly smaller toward the bottom using a scale factor, though I need to check if scaling happens before or after orientation is applied.

Now I'm defining a custom paint function for the dragon bone material that blends ivory tones using noise for mottling, adds darker grain streaks, and cools the underside color using the surface normal's y-component to simulate ambient occlusion.

For the other materials, I'm planning a striped paint for the dark purple cloth using diagonal stripe patterns, and considering whether to use the kit's built-in metal/glow functions for gold versus writing my own gold paint for finer control — I'll likely write my own gold paint but still import the glow helper from the kit.

Now I'm thinking through the remaining accessory pieces: collar rings, a heel mount plate, and ornamental rune bands, plus deciding on texture counts between 5-12, including a blade texture with glowing wisps and runes and a separate glowing rune band texture wrapped around a cylinder for the collar.

For the rest, I'm planning wisp flame-shaped cards rising ghost-like from the blade edge with glow applied, a blade texture possibly including tiny ghostly screaming skull faces, and a gold medallion disc with a dragon-eye sigil mounted on the collar or forehead area.

Beyond that, I want a glowing teal orb at the bottom with swirling line textures on a sphere, and tattered spectral banner cards hanging from the grip collar with purple cloth, gold trim, and rune detailing for added texture variety.

For hardware, I'm adding gold fittings: bands at the grip ends, a heel mount plate with a teal gem at the shaft-blade junction, and gold-capped bone knobs along dorsal spikes on the spine. I'll place a glowing teal octahedron gem at the junction and another on the skull's forehead for focal highlights.

For ghost souls, I'm placing wisps drifting from the blade's inner edge and along the spine top, rising and curling back, rather than flames licking the cutting edge like a typical LoL spirit weapon. For the hanging cards, I'm sizing them small, flowing along a backward-leaning path with some bend, and using cross:true with a side-facing flow so they read clearly from the main viewing angle rather than appearing edge-on.

Now I'm figuring out frame placement for the wisps — anchoring them along the spine's top path with an upward offset from centerline, tilting their direction via lean so they drift up and back, plus considering a larger soul flame near the tip. I'm also sketching a spiky dorsal ridge along the spine by sampling points along the top path and computing an outward-pointing normal from the tangent at each point.

Writing spike generation code...

Then I'm planning the gold socket collar where the shaft connects near the skull, running through the blade heel up toward the top of the shaft.

Adding a back dragon-horn counterbalance for silhouette, then thinking about hanging cloth banners from a collar ring below the skull.

Working out the banner orientation...

So the attachment edge is the drawing's bottom, meaning I need to draw the banner with tatters at the top of the SVG and attachment at the bottom so it hangs correctly when viewed from outside, with the runes drawn upside-down so they read upright once hung.

Now I'm working out the coordinate mapping for the blade texture, converting the outline's bounding box into UV space and then into SVG coordinates with the vertical axis flipped so the tip lands correctly.

Rather than fighting curved gradients inside a rectangle, I realize I can generate an SVG path directly from the sampled outline points, use it as a clip path, then fill the interior with a deep teal gradient and add flowing wisp lines parallel to the edges to suggest soul energy brightest near the cutting edge.

I'm planning a color ramp from deep teal-blue near the spine through cyan to near-white at the cut edge, built as filled polygon bands following the blade's curves, plus a few small circular sigils placed at scattered points along the surface for decorative detail.

Both the top and bottom edge paths start from different heel points but converge at the same tip, so I'm making sure the band geometry narrows correctly near the heel and tapers cleanly to that shared tip. I'm skipping transparency tricks for the edge and just computing the bounding box of all sampled points so I can map the texture coordinates and SVG output consistently across both extruded caps.

Writing extrusion and UV mapping code...

Now I'm designing a wisp SVG as a teardrop flame shape, with nested layers going from deep teal on the outside to white at the core, giving it a glowing gradient look.

Next I'm starting a banner SVG with a jagged-topped dark plum body attached at the bottom of the viewBox.

The teal glyphs should emit light while the dark and gold portions stay unlit, so I'll apply a glow strength to the texture overall. For the medallion, I'm designing a gold ring with a dark center and a teal dragon-eye slit, mounted as a disc on the shaft's front collar face.

For the orb, I'll texture a sphere with a teal gradient and white swirl wisps wrapped around it. I'm also adding soul-fire glow details: a flat teal gem, glowing eye spheres, nostril glow, and a thin glowing plane between the jaws for the mouth cavity fire.

Now I'm thinking through imports and color constants, pulling in the builder's utilities like mix, noise, paint, gradient, and glow kit, then setting up the bone color palette for the skull parts.

Defining bone paint shaders...

Now I'm defining the gold paint shader, blending warm ochre and bright highlight tones with a dark edge falloff, then thinking about the cloth wrap paint using a diagonal spiral sweep based on surface coordinates.

I'm computing a spiral stripe pattern across the wrap's length—mapping coordinates into repeating bands for a cord-like stripe effect in plum and ember-purple tones, then moving on to consider whether the horn/skull paint needs a gradient toward darker tips.

Now I'm setting up the builder with a scythe joint hierarchy—root joint for the spine, a blade joint parented to root, then skull and jaw joints attached to the shaft, making sure names stay unique and only the head/jaw joints carry explicit roles.

Writing shaft and blade coordinates... I'm defining the blade's curve points for top and bottom edges and converting them into 3D positions using a helper that offsets from the blade origin, then building catmull-rom spline paths through those points, checking that the heel of the blade aligns with the shaft radius.

Building outline from paths...

So top sits to the right of bottom at the same y-value, confirming top is the outer convex edge and bottom the inner one, with no crossing in the polygon. I'm checking that equal-t sampling on both curves still produces a valid non-self-intersecting shape for the texture bands.

I'm computing a bounding box from the outline (minX, maxX, minY, maxY) and mapping those coordinates into normalized UV space on a proportionally-scaled SVG viewBox so the texels stay isotropic regardless of the blade's aspect ratio.

Now I'm interpolating between the top and bottom sampled point arrays at fixed band thresholds (from spine to edge) to build polygon strips, each filled with a gradient color and a thin matching stroke to hide seams between bands.

I'm also planning thin white flow lines along band midpoints, small sigil circles with rings and crosses at certain parameter positions, and faint motes near the edge, while making sure the edge side is bright and the spine side stays dark to blend with the bone. I'm double-checking the extrusion rotation math so the local x-axis maps correctly to the world z-axis.

Now I'm working out which world direction the front and back caps face after rotation, so I can figure out the correct "right" and "up" vectors for mapping UV coordinates onto the cap textures from the viewer's perspective.

I'm also checking that the extrude geometry caps work correctly on both sides for culling and alpha materials, then moving on to sweep a thin bone-colored strip along the bottom edge of the blade for a rim detail.

Writing spine sweep code...

Placing the gold rings so their axis follows the tangent direction, spacing them along the spine at several t-values with knuckle spheres interspersed, and defining a radius interpolation function so the rings scale proportionally to the spine's thickness at each point.

Then I'm placing the torus along the tapered tube, and working out strut curves from the hub to points along the top path, picking control points that curve the struts slightly concave to echo the cutting edge while checking they don't cross each other near the tip.

Checking whether a strut heading to the far point pokes outside the blade boundary at a given cross-section — it does, since the strut's y-value dips below the blade's lower edge there. So instead I'm anchoring the hub near the heel's bottom edge and bowing the control points upward toward the spine, which should keep the strut fan contained within the blade outline.

I'm checking whether a simple bezier curve for each strut stays inside the blade's crescent shape, since the bottom edge bulges toward the spine in the middle, making the region non-convex and risking the chord poking through the inner edge.

Testing a few sample points along the chord shows it stays close to the edge but acceptable, so I'll bow the control point up slightly for safety and set the strut radius tapering from 0.016 to 0.007. Now I'm moving on to the hub plate — a gold shield extruded around the heel outline on both front and back sides with some thickness.

Checking the plate shape and placement, I realize its bottom edge at u=-0.18 lands right where the skull sits, so I need to lower the skull's position to avoid a collision between the gold plate and the head.

Adjusting the skull to y=1.64 so it reads as holding the blade, with the top of its head around 1.67 and jaw bottom at 1.49, leaving clearance under the plate bottom at 1.70. I'm also routing the horns to sweep back and up toward the plate, passing near it without intersecting, and considering where to place a small glowing gem on the plate's front face relative to its thickness.

Still shaping skull geometry...

Placing dark eye socket spheres with smaller teal glow orbs just forward of them, and I'm checking that these positions actually sit on the cranium's ellipsoid surface by normalizing coordinates against its semi-axes.

I'll place a dark sphere embedded at each socket with a smaller glow sphere slightly forward for depth. For the horns, I'm defining a backward-curving bezier path from base to tip with tapering radius for each side.

The horns extend upward near the plate region but stay outside it, overlapping nicely for silhouette purposes. I'll add smaller cheek spikes angled outward, and ring bands (small tori) at a point along each horn's tangent to break up the taper with a gold accent.

Now I'm placing the upper teeth as a row of bone-colored spikes along the snout, with x-position and height tapering to match the snout's narrowing width and curving bottom edge, with one tooth extended as a fang.

Next I'm adding front tip teeth at the snout's end, then building the lower jaw as a tapered frustum box hinged near the base, sizing it so there's a natural gap between upper and lower jaw for an open-mouth resting pose.

Now placing a forehead gem: a glowing teal octahedron set at the cranium's peak with a gold setting ring, positioned by calculating where the dome surface sits at that z-offset. Next I'm starting on the skull crest ridge along the spine.

Adding a few small spikes along the top of the cranium pointing backward, skipping the back neck frill since the horns already provide enough detail. For attaching the skull to the shaft, I'm checking the geometry overlap -- the cranium's rear needs to snug around the shaft radius, so repositioning the skull's origin slightly forward to z=0.07 keeps everything flush, with a gold collar ring wrapping the shaft right under the skull.

I'm also working out the shaft layout from bottom to top: talon cage and orb near the base, then a gold ferrule ring, vertebrae section, grip wrap, and finally hanging gold banners near the collar that drape down over the grip area without colliding with the jaw.

I'm also planning gold rune band tubes partway up the shaft and a flat medallion disc set into the grip front, sizing it to sit tangent against the grip's cylindrical surface.

For the spine vertebrae, I'm working out spacing so they're taller and chunkier with visible glowing gaps between segments, dividing them into lower and upper zones of four vertebrae each with roughly 0.07 spacing.

For each vertebra I'm adding small transverse spike processes pointing outward and slightly downward on both sides, plus back spikes, and now I want to define the shaft's curvature as a slight S-curve using a catmull-rom path so vertebra positions stay consistent along it.

Now I'm sweeping a glowing teal core along that shaft path, with a separate wrapped grip section swept at a wider radius between two points on the shaft, and adding gold torus rings at both ends to cap the grip.

For assigning parts to bones, I'll rely on nearest-joint defaults for most elements but explicitly specify the bone for skull, jaw, and blade pieces since their proximity could cause ambiguous joint selection.

Setting up the orb glow sphere and talon wrap geometry now, computing the curved talon positions around the collar base using angular offsets.

Tripod stance looks stable with three contact points, so I'll drop the central spike and add small gold knuckle rings at the joints instead. Skipping dorsal spikes on the talons, and now sketching wisp frames spaced along the top of the spine to texture the blade.

Now I'm making those wisps grow upward then lean back with a varied flow, sizing them smaller near the base and larger at the tip, and considering adding drifting soul-orb wisps near the blade's edge for a stylized spiritual effect while keeping them close rather than fully floating away.

I'll keep things minimal: maybe five tiny glowing motes beneath the cutting edge with trailing wisps, staying within a tenth of the blade. I'm also double-checking the overall silhouette height stays realistic for a scythe, confirming the talons touch the ground at y=0, and noting the skull's tooth color for later use.

Now I'm placing the rune band and spine segments along the shaft, working out exact y-positions so the carved vertebrae, rune ring, and neck collar sit evenly spaced without overlapping the grip or skull geometry below.

I'm defining a banner collar torus just above the shaft, then sketching the gold ferrule as a lathed profile with a tapered cap shape near the lower rune band.

Next I'm designing a back horn counterweight using a bezier sweep that curves backward and upward into a hooked spike, with a gold ring and ridges but skipping any gem accent. Then I'm checking the mid-shaft gap and thinking about adding a teal stripe accent.

For the glowing teal effect, I decide small sphere runes placed symmetrically at intervals along the spine between rings make more sense than painted cracks. I'm also starting to look at the card-frame creation API, figuring out how frames and directions get set up for the glow mesh array.

Then I shift to being careful about TypeScript strictness — avoiding unused imports and locals so the typecheck doesn't reject the build. I start writing the SVG blade builder, defining a helper to interpolate between 2D points and sampling points along the top and bottom paths to construct the outline shape.

Writing SVG color bands...

Adding sigil markers and flow lines...

Checking stroke widths against raster scale to make sure minimum line thickness survives rasterization, so I'm picking an export size around 1024px with roughly 2x scale, then sizing the wisp and rune band viewBoxes accordingly.

Still writing SVG code...

I'm also tallying up the part counts for the skeleton pieces -- vertebrae, processes, spine knobs, rings, motes, and dorsal spikes -- to keep the asset scope organized.

I'm expanding the breakdown to include struts, plates, gems, skull segments, talons, and orb components, pushing the total toward roughly 170 parts with extra details like rib hooks, gold studs, and bone ridges. Now I'm setting up a helper function for 3D vector coordinates.

Writing spike helper for teeth...

I'm checking whether the Joint type is actually exported from the builder module so I can type the bone parameter without errors, and confirming that path.at(t) returns a plain Vector3 rather than a chain point structure.

Now I'm computing a spine coordinate frame at each t by sampling the path's position and tangent, then deriving a perpendicular normal in the y-z plane and verifying it points correctly at both flat and descending tangent orientations. With that frame I'm placing dorsal spikes along the normal offset from the spine curve.

I'm sketching out spike geometry (length/radius tapering with t), spike count and spacing along the blade, plus wisp and mote particle placements near the spine and blade edge. Then I'm starting to lay out the actual module code: imports from the builder library, the meta export with name/description, and a constants object to hold shared values before writing the full implementation.

Now I'm defining a paint function for the wrap texture that colors bands based on a position/slice value, then beginning the main build function that sets up the rigid joint hierarchy -- root, blade, skull, jaw -- establishing positions and orientations for the scythe's skeletal frame.

Writing shaft sweep geometry...

The core glow should stay hidden mostly, peeking through gaps near the waist where the vertebra lathe profile is thinner than the shaft radius, so I'm building the lathe profile for each vertebra segment to make sure the taper matches up correctly at the joints.

Placing vertebrae along the shaft curve...

Adding outward-pointing spikes and considering small glowing accents on the front of upper vertebrae for visual detail.

Now I'm working on the grip wrap sweep along the shaft path, sizing the radius and assigning it to the root bone, then adding gold rings at the grip ends with a possible medallion band at the midpoint.

Placing the medallion itself with a backing gold disc and a textured plane, figuring out the exact z-offsets so it sits flush against the shaft's slight curvature at that height.

I'm working through the runeband placement at the shaft, then sketching a collar ring near the banners and considering a gold flared lathe shape under the skull as a socket collar, checking it clears the jaw geometry.

Now I'm pinning down the skull's coordinates — setting a skull center point, a jaw hinge position below it, and confirming the cranium's lower ellipsoid bottom aligns with the collar top. I'm also laying out the jaw box between the hinge and an endpoint, and starting the upper snout points relative to the skull center.

Checking that the jaw and snout gaps give a believable open-mouth look — the snout bottom and jaw top leave about a 0.07 gap at the front, confirming the mouth reads as open while staying closed near the hinge. Now I'm moving on to placing teeth.

Positioning upper teeth along the snout with interpolated widths and lengths, including a longer fang, then adding lower teeth along the jaw line with their own fang and a downward-pointing chin spike.

Now I'm placing the eye sockets and teal eye spheres symmetrically, plus brow rods above each eye, checking whether the brow endpoints sit correctly relative to the cranium and snout geometry.

The brow rod ends up near the eye socket at x=0.047, creating a shading overlap that reads well since the eyes point outward and forward. Now I'm checking horn base placement at the cranium's top-back, verifying whether that position falls inside the ellipsoid boundary.

Confirming the horn bases sit just slightly inside the cranium surface for a natural buried look, then sketching the bezier curve for each horn with control points sweeping outward and up, tapering radius from 0.03 to a point and adding reinforcing rings along the shaft. Checking clearance against the blade's rear horn and plate thickness to avoid collisions, then moving on to define cheek spikes using similar directional vector parameters.

Now I'm placing the cranium mesh itself, scaling a low-poly sphere to shape the skull, and positioning a glowing teal gem embedded in the forehead with a gold ring around it -- recalculating the exact surface height at that point so the gem sits half-buried rather than floating. I'm also working out the ridge spike positions along the cranium's curve, computing the surface height at each z-offset so the spikes emerge naturally from the dome rather than poking through at the wrong depth.

Now I'm sketching the mouth's inner glow, placing a small flattened teal sphere between the jaws to suggest soul-fire light, and solving for the jaw surface height at that point so the glow sits correctly inside the mouth cavity rather than clipping through the jaw mesh.

I'm adding a rising wisp card above the mouth to evoke flame escaping, then planning rear hinge cap geometry and a spine sweep along the top path with a tapered radius function and rounded-to-pointed end caps.

I'm positioning bone knuckle spheres along the spine at specific parameter points, then layering gold tendon rings between them, and working out where to place teal glow dots on the knuckle flanks so they don't overlap the rings.

Now I'm sketching the plate outline as a closed polygon of heel points with some thickness, checking whether the vertex order is consistent for the shape to render correctly.

I'll bevel the edges slightly for safety, then set the extrude position and bone attachment with the gold color, before adding small gold studs along scaled-in outline points on either side face and placing gem accents near the center.

Now I'm adding support struts swept as bezier curves between root points on the bottom path and corresponding points on the top path, bowed slightly outward with a mid control point, colored bone and attached to the blade bone with rounded caps. I'm also adding small knob spheres at the strut roots and considering a thinner secondary rod along the spine's inner edge.

I'm shaping a back horn as a tapered sweep curving upward from the spine base, then setting up four hanging banner cards arranged in a ring around the figure, each oriented outward with a flow direction function so they face away from the center with some randomized variation.

I'm choosing angles of 0, 90, 180, 270 degrees for the banner positions so that two banners appear face-on from the side view and two from the front view, computing each banner's x/z offset from the angle using sine and cosine.

I'm checking that the banner hangs between the grip medallion and rune band without overlapping either, confirming clearance along the vertical axis. For the wisp elements, I'm orienting each one along the outward normal of the spine curve, then tilting it slightly toward the flow direction projected onto the surface.

For the tip wisp I'm making a larger flame-like shape pointing along the tangent instead of the normal, and for motes I'm scattering small glowing spheres along the bottom path at a handful of parametric points with slight downward offsets to suggest falling embers.

I'm also thinking each mote could trail a small downward-facing wisp card beneath it, like a tail, so the orb reads as a soul with a faint streak -- sized small and cross-planed for visibility. I'll skip adding a floor or point light, and move on to double-checking the skull sphere glow counts before writing the final code, including a torus helper function for bone-based geometry placement.

Setting up constants and color types, then assembling the blade's module-level structure with texture generation deferred into the build function for safety. Writing module code...

Building the blade geometry by extruding the outline shape, then computing UV coordinates per vertex for texture mapping...

Checking that glow accepts Sweep and card meshes correctly, and confirming the fallback logic when a target lacks isMesh or meshes properties resolves to using its single mesh reference, which should typecheck fine for Part objects.

I'm deciding to skip unused helpers like stick and surface since they aren't required by the brief, and confirming the sweep/lathe part calls use the right option shapes with position, direction, segment count, and bone references.

Now I'm writing the talon geometry loop, computing three claw positions spaced around the foot with bezier paths that taper from a wide base to a sharp point, using a sweep with a point-capped tip so each claw ends exactly at zero radius, then adding a small gold ring partway down each claw as a decorative band.

I'm placing a joint knob at the talon root, then working out the ferrule lathe profile that sits above the talons, and adjusting where the shaft core starts so it doesn't float awkwardly through the orb cage — settling on starting it at y=0.17 so it reads as descending naturally into the orb.

Now I'm checking the orb's position and radius against the talon curve's width at the midpoint to make sure the talons wrap the orb convincingly, then starting to sketch the banner shape as an SVG path.

Writing SVG code...

I need strokes to be at least 3px, so I'm bumping the size up to 256 with a 1.6 scale factor to keep lines visible, then moving on to building the wisp SVG shape.

Still writing SVG code...

Still writing icon path data...

Adding swirl details to the orb gradient, then double-checking the bezier helper accepts point arrays correctly before moving to the rng signature — making sure rng returns a callable number generator I can pass into the card setup.

For the mote wisps, I'm orienting the flame card to point downward from the mote so it reads as a trailing comet shape, tuning glow strength values, and tightening TypeScript strictness with const assertions on the arrays.
